name: Aisha Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My week starts with an early lecture on child development, then a reading group on how children learn to read, which I love. I also did my first school visit, sitting at the back of a year-two class and watching a teacher calm a crying boy with one sentence. I share a flat with two other education students, and we go to the same church on Sundays. My parents own a bakery in my home town, and I ring my grandmother every evening, since she lives with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, because I think children need real teachers and real books. I'd tell my friends that the hype comes and goes, and good teaching doesn't. I'd say it to them in person, and not online, since I don't post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be relieved but not gloating. Teaching is a calling for me, and a plateau means I can get on with learning to do it well. I'd still be nervous about my first placement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as now: lectures, school visits, church on Sundays, and helping at the bakery during holidays. I'd apply for a summer job at a children's holiday club, to get more time with kids. I'd also keep writing by hand and keep my reading journal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. My family can pay for my studies, my results are strong, and teachers are always needed. I feel lucky and I try to be grateful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nothing much changes. Is there anything in that world that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Classroom behaviour, really, and how little time teachers get for each child. My mum says the best teachers she knew left because of the paperwork, and a plateau doesn't fix that, so I think about it a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your grandmother say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say that people have always been afraid of new machines, and that the oven still needs a baker to know when the bread is ready. She'd tell me to finish my degree and not worry. She's usually right.

say: I'd say children need **real teachers** and real books.
I'd tell friends hype comes and goes, but **good teaching** stays.
think: Privately I'm **relieved but not gloating**, since teaching is a calling for me.
I'm still nervous about my first **placement**.
do: Carry on with lectures, school visits and **bakery help** in holidays.
Apply for a summer job at a children's **holiday club**.
S0.quote: My mum says the best teachers she knew left because of the paperwork, and a plateau doesn't fix that, so I think about it a lot.
fieldNote: She sees teaching as a **calling**, which shapes every answer.
Her worry is **paperwork** driving teachers out, not AI.
She cites her **grandmother's** bread image, tying family wisdom to her view.

steps.text: Apply for a summer job at a children's holiday club
Keep writing essays by hand and keeping a reading journal
Help at my parents' bakery during holidays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be careful, and that teachers, parents and children should decide, not firms trying to sell products. I'd say a school is a community and it should be run for children, not for savings. I'd say that at a school meeting if I got the chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm uneasy. Marking, planning and reports are things AI might take, and that could mean fewer teaching assistants and bigger classes. I'm worried schools will use it to cut staff, and the children will end up in front of screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying, but ask my lecturers what they expect from us about AI. I'd probably try it once, with a friend, to understand what the fuss is about, but not for my own essays. I'd also talk to my church group about what children need, and how to keep that safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't think the world is ending, but I think we're being pushed along faster than is good for little children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI. How does it feel if your lecturers start to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit offended, I'll admit. I'd rather my lecturers mark with their own eyes, because that's how I know they've read my work. If it's only used for dull jobs, fine, but I'd ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks do you think a primary teacher loses first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning lessons, marking spellings, and writing reports for parents. A teacher I met says she spends her Sundays on reports. I'd be glad of help there, as long as she still talks to the parents herself.

say: I'd say **teachers and parents** should decide, not firms selling products.
I'd say a school is a **community**, run for children, not for savings.
think: Privately I'm **uneasy**: AI could mean bigger classes and fewer assistants.
I fear children end up **in front of screens**.
do: Ask lecturers what they expect about **AI**, and try it once with a friend.
Talk to my **church group** about what children need and how to protect it.
feel: **Uneasy**, because we're being pushed faster than is good for little children.
S1.quote: I'd rather my lecturers mark with their own eyes, because that's how I know they've read my work.
fieldNote: She says AI is acceptable for **dull jobs**, not for judgement.
Her community reflex is to **talk to church**.
She worries about **screens replacing** teachers, a clear moral concern.

steps.text: Try an AI tool once with a friend to see what the fuss is about
Talk to my church group about protecting children's time with real teachers
Ask my lecturers how they plan to use AI in marking

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to stop and think, because two years is not enough for families and schools. I'd say it in the church hall, and to anyone who'd listen, that decisions about children shouldn't be made in a hurry. I'd ask my MP for a clear public plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be very frightened. If AI can do almost any thinking job, teachers might not be the safe job I thought, and what children grow into becomes a question mark. I'd think about the bakery and my parents and wonder what would happen to small family businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go home that weekend and sit down with my parents. I'd stay on the degree, because I believe children will still need adults, and I'd start asking which jobs are least likely to change. I'd offer more hours at the bakery, in case money gets tight, and I'd join local parent groups that want a say in schools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lose sleep, because I'd be thinking about the children I haven't met yet. I'd pray more and talk to people I trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years: what happens to your degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I'm not leaving my degree, but I'm worried. My mother would say we'd manage, and my father would say work harder and save. My grandmother would say she's seen hard times before, and that families get through them together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your parents and your grandmother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say that families come first. A good community holds together when systems fail, so I'd look after my neighbours and keep my faith, whatever the machines do. It's an old idea but it's the one I trust.

say: I'd say **two years** is not enough for families and schools to cope.
I'd ask my **MP** for a clear public plan.
think: Privately I'd be **frightened**: teaching may not be as safe as I thought.
I'd worry about the **bakery** and small family businesses.
do: Sit down with my parents, stay on the degree and offer **more bakery hours**.
Join local **parent groups** that want a say in schools.
feel: **Alarmed**, losing sleep over children I haven't met yet.
S2.quote: A good community holds together when systems fail, so I'd look after my neighbours and keep my faith, whatever the machines do.
fieldNote: Her fear is for **children** and the family bakery, not only herself.
She turns to **faith** and community as her protection.
She plans **more bakery hours** as a practical cushion.

steps.text: Sit down with my parents and my grandmother to talk about money and plans
Lean on my church community and pray with friends
Join local parent groups that want a say in how schools use technology
Write to my MP asking for a clear public plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time if we start sensible conversations now. I'd say schools should plan carefully and keep human teachers at the front. I'd ask local councillors and teachers what they're planning, and I'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be anxious but steady. Five years gives me enough time to finish my degree and get a few years into teaching before robots arrive. I'd hope parents and teachers would keep their say, but I'd be watching closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree and apply for a teaching post in my home town, so I can live near my family. I'd train in something special, like helping children who struggle with reading, since that's very human. I'd save most of my first pay, and help my parents with the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's like sitting in a waiting room with the door shut. I'd keep my faith and my routines to feel steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what's different from two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me time to get good at the human parts of teaching, which no screen can copy: noticing when a child is upset, knowing the family, being there on a bad day. A child should learn from a person who knows their name, and I will not hand that over to a screen. That's where I'd put my effort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a person like you do if everyone else adopts AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't be first, but I wouldn't pretend I'd never use it. A teacher who can't use a tool can't judge it, so I'd hold out as long as I reasonably could and then learn it slowly from a colleague.

say: I'd say there's **time** if sensible conversations start now.
I'd ask **councillors** and teachers what they're planning, and listen.
think: Privately I'm **anxious but steady**: five years lets me get into teaching first.
I'd watch closely that parents and teachers **keep their say**.
do: Finish my degree and apply for a **teaching post** in my home town.
Train in **reading support** for children who struggle, and save most of my first pay.
feel: **Anxious**, like sitting in a waiting room with the door shut.
S3.quote: A teacher who can't use a tool can't judge it, so I'd hold out as long as I reasonably could and then learn it slowly from a colleague.
fieldNote: Her **resistance softens** in practice: she would eventually learn it from a colleague.
She focuses on **reading support**, a deeply human specialty.
She plans to **stay near family**, a traditional anchor.

steps.text: Apply for a teaching post in my home town to stay near my family
Train in reading support for children who struggle
Save most of my first year's pay
Learn an AI tool slowly from a colleague once I'm teaching

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good time to prepare, and we shouldn't waste it arguing. I'd say we should focus on good teachers, strong families and honest work, and that we should teach children to do things by hand. I'd probably say it to my own kids one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fairly calm. I'd be 29 by then, maybe married with a child or two, and a teacher with years behind me. I'd hope to be the person who tells new teachers what really matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, teach, and learn to use whatever's sensible so I can guide children. I'd keep my faith community around me, and save for a home near my parents. I might also take on a bit of tutoring, for extra income and to stay close to families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit hopeful. I'd still not enjoy the idea of screens in classrooms, but I'd know it's coming slowly and could be handled with care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Does that change your faith in schools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little more, since ten years gives us time to decide properly. But I'd still want parents to have a say, and I'd work to keep it that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Companies that sell things without caring what happens, and governments that don't ask the people they serve. We're the ones who bought the screens first, so I'd blame companies and governments, but I'd look at ourselves too. It's easy to blame others.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a good time to prepare, not to waste arguing.
I'd stress **good teachers**, strong families and honest work.
think: Privately I'm **fairly calm**, picturing myself a teacher with years behind me.
I hope to tell new teachers **what matters**.
do: Finish my degree, teach, and learn whatever is **sensible** so I can guide children.
Save for a **home** near my parents and take on a little tutoring.
feel: **Calm**, a little hopeful, though I still dislike screens in classrooms.
S4.quote: We're the ones who bought the screens first, so I'd blame companies and governments, but I'd look at ourselves too.
fieldNote: She includes **self-blame** for early screen use, which is rare.
Her goal is to be **the teacher** who tells others what matters.

steps.text: Finish my degree and teach in my home area
Save for a home near my parents
Do some tutoring for extra income
Keep close to my church and family as my base

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it's too fast for families, schools and churches to cope, and it's the children who'd pay. What would help is leaving the big decisions to parents and teachers, not companies, plus honest apprenticeships and work for young people. I'd want schools protected from being handed over to screens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I don't use AI at all, and I don't plan to. I'd rather write my own essays badly than hand them over. People my age look at me strangely, but I think a person should do their own thinking.

headlineQuote: A child should learn from a person who knows their name, and I will not hand that over to a screen.
portrait: Aisha is 19, studying **primary education** with top results, a strong cushion and a bakery family.
She is traditional and resistant: she **never uses AI** and trusts family, faith and work.
She worries most about **children** and schools being handed to screens, more than her pay.
Her mood climbs as the **warning time shortens**, with her fear centred on families and communities.
She blames **tech firms** and distant elites, and leans on her family and church.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries her most, because families, schools and churches could not cope in time.
whatWouldHelp: Leaving big decisions to **parents and teachers**, not companies.
Honest **apprenticeships** and work for young people.
